title: The road on the Annapurna Circuit and the trails around it
meta_description: How jeep roads changed the Annapurna Circuit, what villagers gained, what trekkers lost, and how the NATT trails and old paths still keep you off the road.
summary: Jeep roads now run up the Marsyangdi to Manang and down the Kali Gandaki from Muktinath. For villages they brought cheaper goods and hospitals within reach; for trekkers they brought dust. But marked NATT trails and old paths on the opposite bank or higher on the slope keep most of the Circuit on foot, if you plan for them.

sections.heading: When the road came
paras: For most of its history, the Annapurna Circuit was a walk between villages that could only be reached on foot or by mule. When the trek opened to foreigners in the late 1970s, it took around three weeks from the Marsyangdi valley over Thorong La and down the Kali Gandaki, and every kilo of rice, kerosene and beer in the lodges came up on someone's back or on a mule train. The trail was the only road.

That changed in the 2000s and 2010s. On the west side, a road was pushed up the Kali Gandaki from Beni through Tatopani to Jomsom, opening to traffic in stages, and then on to Muktinath. On the east side, a jeep track was cut from Besisahar up the Marsyangdi gorge, reaching Chame and later Manang. Today you can sit in a jeep from Besisahar to Manang, cross Thorong La on foot, and take another jeep from Muktinath to Jomsom and Pokhara. The pass itself, at 5,416 m, is still crossed only on foot or on horseback.

sections.heading: What the road changed
paras: For people living in these valleys, the road is mostly a blessing. A sack of rice that once cost a week's porterage now arrives by truck. A pregnant woman or an injured farmer can reach the hospital in Besisahar, Beni or Pokhara in hours, not days. Apples from Marpha and potatoes from Manang can be sold in Pokhara before they spoil. Families who once sent children away to school can visit them more often. When trekkers complain about the road, villagers sometimes smile and ask how many days the trekker would carry a gas cylinder up from Besisahar.

For trekkers, the road brought dust, engine noise and jeeps on the narrow sections of the old trail. Some lodges on the lower Kali Gandaki, which once lived on trekkers walking down from Jomsom, lost much of that trade when people began taking jeeps instead. For a few years the Circuit was written off in travel articles as ruined. That was too quick: the mountains, villages and the pass are still there, and so are most of the footpaths, if you know where to find them.

The road also changed who comes. Indian and Nepali pilgrims now reach Muktinath by jeep in large numbers, especially in spring and autumn, and the lodges of Ranipauwa below the temple have grown to serve them. On a busy morning the temple courtyard holds more pilgrims than trekkers, and that is a good thing to see: Muktinath was a pilgrimage place for centuries before anyone came to walk around the Annapurnas.

sections.heading: The NATT trails
paras: In response, the Annapurna Conservation Area Project and trekking groups marked a set of alternative footpaths known as the NATT, the New Annapurna Trekking Trails. They link old village paths, herders' tracks and new sections on the opposite bank of the river or higher on the slopes, so trekkers can walk most of the Circuit away from vehicles. The routes are painted with trail markers on rocks and walls, usually red and white, with blue and white on some side trails.

The NATT routes are often harder than walking the road: steeper, longer and sometimes with extra climbs. They are also more beautiful, with better views, more villages, and the quiet that the Circuit was famous for. A good guide knows which sections are worth the extra effort and which are washed out or overgrown that season.

Not every NATT section is open every year. Monsoon rains bring down bridges and landslides, and some side paths fall out of use when lodges along them close. Ask in the villages. Lodge owners know which paths their own guests used last week, and they are usually honest about which ones to avoid.

sections.heading: Road sections and trail alternatives
paras: The table below shows the main places where road and trail part company, as we know them. Conditions change after every monsoon, so treat it as a starting point and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Walking the east side
paras: On the Marsyangdi side, the most important choice is above Pisang. The road and the lower trail follow the valley floor through Humde to Manang. The upper route climbs steeply from the river to Ghyaru, about 3,670 m, then contours through Ngawal and Braga to Manang. It is one of the finest walks in Nepal, with Annapurna II, III and IV and Gangapurna in a line across the valley, old stone villages with prayer walls, and a useful extra night high up that helps acclimatisation.

Lower down, the high trail via Timang and Thanchowk between Dharapani and Koto avoids a long stretch of road and gives early views of Manaslu and Annapurna II. Many trekkers now start walking at Chamje or Dharapani after a jeep ride, accepting that the lowest gorge section is mostly road.

Between Bhratang and Pisang, where the valley bends below the great curved rock slab of Paungda Danda, the trail and road run close together, but there are footpaths on the far bank for parts of the way. Your guide will choose depending on dust, traffic and how the legs feel; on this stretch, a short ride is no great loss.

sections.heading: Walking the west side
paras: After Thorong La, many trekkers take a jeep from Muktinath and fly or drive out from Jomsom. That is a pity, because the Kali Gandaki side has some of the best villages in the region. From Muktinath an alternative path leads over a ridge to Lubra, a village known for its Bon monastery, then down the Panda Khola to the Kali Gandaki near Jomsom. Kagbeni, with its mud-brick lanes and old monastery, can be reached on footpaths rather than the road.

South of Jomsom, the east bank trail leads to Marpha, a Thakali village of whitewashed houses, apple orchards and a famous brandy, and on to Tukuche, once a great salt-trading town. Further down, trails through Larjung, Kokhethanti and Titi lake keep you off the road with views of Dhaulagiri and Nilgiri. Walking all the way to Tatopani and up to Ghorepani turns the Circuit into a three-week classic again.

sections.heading: How we plan it now
paras: We no longer pretend the road is not there. We use it where walking it would add nothing, and leave it wherever a real trail exists.

Most importantly, we treat the road as a tool, not a verdict. A trekker who walks from Chame to Muktinath on trails, stays two nights in Manang and walks down to Kagbeni has had a great Annapurna trek, whatever drove past on the far bank. If anything, the road has made the Circuit easier to fit into two weeks, and the parts that matter most have not changed at all.
list: Jeep from Besisahar to Chamje or Dharapani to skip the dustiest section.
Walk the high trail via Timang where conditions allow.
Always take the upper route via Ghyaru and Ngawal to Manang.
Two nights in Manang and short days to Thorong Phedi.
After the pass, walk to Kagbeni and Jomsom on paths, or via Lubra.
Fly from Jomsom, or keep walking south on the NATT if you have time.

faqs.q: Is the Annapurna Circuit still worth doing with the road?
faqs.a: Yes. The road has changed the lower valleys, but the walk from Pisang through Ngawal and Manang to Thorong La and Muktinath is still entirely on trails, and the scenery and cultures are as remarkable as ever. Using a jeep for the dustiest sections and the NATT trails elsewhere keeps the trek a real walk.

NATT stands for New Annapurna Trekking Trails, a set of marked footpaths created to let trekkers avoid the jeep roads on the Annapurna Circuit. They use old village paths and new sections on the opposite riverbank or higher slopes, and are marked with painted trail signs. They are often steeper than the road but quieter and more scenic.

Yes. A jeep road runs from Besisahar up the Marsyangdi valley to Manang, served by local jeeps, though it is rough and can be blocked by landslides, especially in the monsoon. Driving straight to Manang at 3,540 m from low altitude is risky for acclimatisation; walking the last days from Chame or Pisang is safer.

faqs.q: Is there a road over Thorong La?
faqs.a: No. Thorong La, at 5,416 m, is crossed only on foot or on horseback. Roads reach Manang on the east side and Muktinath on the west, but the stretch between, via Yak Kharka, Thorong Phedi and the pass, is trail only. This is the heart of the Circuit and remains a serious high-altitude walk.

faqs.q: Should I take a jeep from Besisahar?
faqs.a: For most trekkers with limited time, yes. The lowest section from Besisahar to Chamje follows a dusty jeep road through a gorge, with only some trail alternatives. A jeep saves one to two days for the more rewarding upper valley. If you have time and want the full walk, old trails via Bhulbhule and Ghermu remain.

faqs.q: What is the best NATT section on the Circuit?
faqs.a: The upper route from Pisang via Ghyaru and Ngawal to Manang is the most rewarding, with views of Annapurna II, III and IV and Gangapurna and old stone villages. On the west side, the path from Muktinath via Lubra to Jomsom and the east bank trail to Marpha are also excellent.

faqs.q: How many days does the Circuit take now?
faqs.a: With a jeep to Chamje or Dharapani and a flight from Jomsom, 12 to 14 days of walking from Kathmandu makes a full trip of about 15 to 16 nights. Walking the whole way from Besisahar and down the Kali Gandaki to Tatopani and Ghorepani takes three weeks or more.

faqs.q: Did the road hurt local lodges?
faqs.a: Some, yes. Lodges on the lower Kali Gandaki lost trade when trekkers began taking jeeps from Jomsom instead of walking down. Others benefited from cheaper supplies and new road travellers, including Indian pilgrims to Muktinath. Choosing to walk the NATT trails and stay in village lodges spreads income back along the route.

faqs.q: Are the NATT trails well marked?
faqs.a: Mostly, with painted markers on rocks, walls and trees, but marks fade, and monsoon landslides wash out sections every year. Some junctions are confusing in cloud. A licensed guide, now required for foreign trekkers in the conservation area, knows the current state of each section. Check current status before you travel.
